newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Netanyahu proposes non-stop Hebron negotiations.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu proposes non-stop Hebron negotiations.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, travelling on Monday to an Arab-Israeli summit in Washington, proposed non-stop talks with the Palestinians on Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank city of Hebron.

"I am proposing that the two sides meet right after the meeting in Washington in a locale to be determined to engage in continuous negotiations until agreement is reached," he told reporters on his plane to the White House summit.
However, Palestinians had already negotiated the Israeli redeployment in Hebron, originally delayed after a wave of Moslem suicide bombings in Israel in February and May.
They had considered carrying out the redeployment a test of the right-wing Netanyahu's willingness to honour pledges since taking office in June to press forward in peace efforts.

Netanyahu said recent Israeli-Palestinian violence, which claimed the lives of 69 Arabs and Jews, would make it imperative to inject security changes into the deal with the previous Israeli government.

"If you were a father or mother to (Jewish) children in Hebron, would you want your security to be ensured by armed Palestinian policemen on the hills," Netanyahu said. "We have to talk about modifications because of the new security situation and I believe this can be achieved with goodwill."

Netanyahu, who made a refuelling stop in Amsterdam, said the proposed negotiations also would focus on an Israeli closure in effect since February in the West Bank and Gaza and "questions of security" including a Gazan airport Palestinians want to run.
"Once agreement is reached on these issues, implementation can be immediate," he said.

Netanyahu said both he and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat would be involved in the decision-making so results would be swift. The Israeli leader said he saw the talks as "simply continuous discussions until the white smoke comes out".
But he said a controversial tunnel in Jerusalem that sparked last week's violence, the worst between Israelis and Palestinians since a landmark peace deal in 1993, "won't be on the agenda".
Palestinian officials have said they will demand at the summit, scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday, that Israel close the tunnel which runs near Islamic holy sites in Jerusalem.

U.S. President Bill Clinton on Sunday invited Netanyahu, Arafat, Jordan's King Hussein and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak to try to defuse tensions that have threatened to destroy the U.S.-brokered Middle East peace process.
But the White House said on Monday that Mubarak, who has waged a war of words with Israel recently over the slow pace of peace, would not go.
Arafat, who had insisted on Mubarak's participation, has yet to say he will attend. The Palestinian leader travelled to Luxembourg to meet European foreign leaders after talks with Mubarak in Egypt.
Netanyahu again accused Arafat of using the opening of the tunnel as an excuse for inciting violence to pressure Israel into concessions.

"I hope to be able to build, rebuild, a new commitment on both sides and to pursue peace peacefully," Netanyahu told reporters on his plane. "I hope we'll be able to rehabilitate the trust between us."
